118	## 3. Vanilla quick play
119	
120	- Minecraft 26.1.2 accepts:
121	  - `--quickPlayPath <file>`, required argument;
122	  - `--quickPlaySingleplayer [world]`, optional argument;
123	  - `--quickPlayMultiplayer <addr>`;
124	  - `--quickPlayRealms <id>`.
125	
126	  Source: `MC:net/minecraft/client/main/Main.java:63-66`.
127	- `QuickPlay.connect` routes to single player (`MC:net/minecraft/client/quickplay/QuickPlay.java:42-70`).
128	  - A blank world id means the most recent world (`:55-58`, `getLatestSingleplayerWorld` after line 70).
129	  - `joinSingleplayerWorld` opens the world if `levelExists(identifier)`. Otherwise it shows an error screen over the world list, and a human or bridge has to handle it (`:87-94`).
130	  - The identifier is the save folder name.
131	- `--quickPlayPath` names a JSON file under the game dir (`MC:net/minecraft/client/quickplay/QuickPlayLog.java:38-40`). It is written after the player has logged in to the world (`:50-77`, called from `MC:net/minecraft/client/multiplayer/ClientPacketListener.java:556`), which would make a clean "joined" signal. Prism does not pass `--quickPlayPath`; it adds only `--quickPlaySingleplayer` or `--quickPlayMultiplayer` (`PRISM:launcher/minecraft/MinecraftInstance.cpp#L758-L769`). Prism's instance settings expose JVM args and env vars (`#L187-L192`, `#L238-L239`) but no game-argument setting was found.
132	- How launchers pass it:
133	  - Prism appends the argument to the game args when the version trait says the version supports it (section 1).
134	  - Older Minecraft versions without the multiplayer trait get `--server`/`--port` instead (`PRISM:libraries/launcher/org/prismlauncher/launcher/impl/StandardLauncher.java#L84-L98`).
135	  - Prism also exposes the final arguments as the system property `org.prismlauncher.launch.gameargs` (`#L108-L111`).
136	
137	## 4. Driving the running game without a human
138	
139	The three items are: (J) the Jade tooltips, (O) the Oracle Index book, and (C) a real unload of part of a multiblock's chunks.
140	
141	| Option | How it works (source) | J | O | C |
142	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
143	| Dev-only bridge mod (recommended) | Structure Lab pattern: HTTP on 127.0.0.1, ephemeral port, bearer token in `connection.json`, started at `FMLClientSetupEvent` (`LabBridge.java:43-66`, `LabCapture.java:24`) | Yes: aim plus `JadeTooltipCollectedCallback` text plus screenshot | Yes: `OracleClient.openEntry`/`openScreen` plus screenshot | Yes: commands plus `level.isLoaded` / `ChunkEvent.Unload` |
144	| Structure Lab as is | Status, block listing and `inspect` work in any world. `submit` and capture need a world made with its preset (`LabSession.java:44-49`, `LabBridge.java:87-89`), and capture hides the HUD and closes screens (`LabCapture.java:35-37`). It freezes ticks only in its own preset world (`LabSession.java:29`, `:41`) | No (HUD hidden) | No (screens closed) | Partly: `inspect` can read block states, but it has no command or teleport op |
145	| Server commands typed by a human-like driver | `/tp`, `/forceload`, `/setblock` and `/place` need cheats. Both ATM11 saves checked have `allowCommands` 1 (`level.dat`). `/stop` and `/save-all` exist only on a dedicated server (`MC:net/minecraft/commands/Commands.java:280-296`) | Setup only | Setup only | Yes, with something to send the commands |
146	| Client commands | NeoForge `RegisterClientCommandsEvent` (`NEO:src/client/java/net/neoforged/neoforge/client/event/RegisterClientCommandsEvent.java`). These are commands the bridge mod could add; they need a way to type them | Via bridge | Via bridge | Via bridge |
147	| RCON | Only `DedicatedServer` starts `RconThread`, when `enable-rcon=true` (`MC:net/minecraft/server/dedicated/DedicatedServer.java:299-302`, `DedicatedServerProperties.java:84`). "Open to LAN" (`/publish`, integrated only, `Commands.java:298-300`) starts a game TCP listener and LAN pinger, not RCON (`MC:net/minecraft/client/server/IntegratedServer.java:223-246`) | No | No | Yes, but only on a dedicated server (dev `just server`), not in a Prism single-player world |
148	| Log tailing | `$INST/<id>/minecraft/logs/latest.log`, with markers such as "joined the game", "Saving and pausing game...", "Stopping server" and "Stopping!" (lines 5313-5449 of the current ATM11 `latest.log`) | Errors only | Errors only (missing pages, resource errors) | Errors only |
149	| F2 / `Screenshot.grab` | F2 works with a screen open (the check in `MC:net/minecraft/client/KeyboardHandler.java:462-485` does not test for a screen) and writes to `<gameDir>/screenshots/` (`instance minecraft/screenshots/` exists) | Yes (HUD on) | Yes | Visual only |
150	| macOS `screencapture` | `-l<windowid>`, `-o`, `-x` (`screencapture -h`) | Yes, if the window is visible | Yes | Visual only |
151	| Computer-use MCP | Screenshots and key or mouse input to a granted app, with the owner's approval per app (this session's computer-use tool rules) | Yes, by reading pixels | Yes | Yes, by typing commands |
152	| NeoForge client test framework | `testframework` has only a manual overlay and test screen for the client (`NEO:testframework/src/main/java/net/neoforged/testframework/client/FrameworkClientImpl.java`, key mappings and a GUI layer). A GitHub code search of NeoForge for "ClientGameTest" found nothing | No | No | No |
153	
154	Notes on the table:
155	
156	- **Jade** draws its overlay only on a physical client and swallows plugin exceptions (`$MP/docs/agents/verifying.md:4`). Any Jade check needs a real client with no screen open, the HUD on and the crosshair on the block. Pause on lost focus defeats all three (`MC:net/minecraft/client/Minecraft.java:1400-1408`). The bridge can set `options.pauseOnLostFocus=false` at runtime, as Structure Lab does (`LabBridge.java:127`), and F3+P toggles the same option (`MC:net/minecraft/client/KeyboardHandler.java:268-270`).
157	- **The chunk unload** needs the integrated server to keep ticking: a paused game pauses it (`MC:net/minecraft/client/server/IntegratedServer.java:125`). In ATM11's `options.txt`, render distance is 16 and simulation distance is 12 (lines 33-34), so the player has to move well beyond 16 chunks, or into another dimension, for the far chunks to unload.
158	
159	## 5. Getting the dev jar into an instance, and the risks
160	
161	- **Copying `build/libs/*.jar` into `all_the_mods_11_atm11/minecraft/mods`** works technically (section 2), but it puts an unreleased jar into the owner's real game. The next normal play of "New World" (1.5 GB, last written Nov 7 04:00) would load and save Planter Blocks and cores with the dev code. The owner's notes ask for a test world copy and asking first (`$MP/NOTES.md:359`). That instance is also a managed CurseForge pack (`instance.cfg:8-13`), so a pack update could change the mod set under the tests.
162	- **Recommended: a dedicated copy of the instance.**
163	  - Sizes: the whole instance is 23 GB. `config` is 8.5 GB, `simplebackups` 7.0 GB, `backups` 3.4 GB, `saves` 1.6 GB and `mods` 856 MB (`du`). The disk has 103 GB free (`df -h`).
164	  - An APFS clone (`/bin/cp -c -R`, or Prism's Copy Instance with Clone) shares blocks until something is written.
165	  - Prism's copy dialog can also leave out saves, mods and the rest (`PRISM:launcher/InstanceCopyPrefs.h#L15-L27`).
166	  - Prism watches the instance dir and finds new folders (`PRISM:launcher/InstanceList.cpp#L79-L82`, `#L470-L489`).
167	  - Copy while the game is closed, because `session.lock` is held by a running world.
168	- **Lighter option: a world copy inside the same instance.** Copy only `saves/New World` to a new folder. This protects the save but not the modpack: the dev jar still sits in the owner's real `mods/`, and every world in that instance loads it.
169	- **The copy's `instance.cfg`** keeps `name=` and `uuid=` from the source (`instance.cfg:27-29`). Two instances would then show the same name in Prism. The ID used by the CLI is still the folder name, so this matters only for the owner's view.
170	
171	## 6. Detecting launch success or failure, and shutting down cleanly
172	
173	**Launch detection**
174	
175	- **Prism's exit code, only when no Prism was running.** Without `--show-window`, Prism opens no window. When the game ends it exits with 0 if the launch succeeded and 1 if it failed (`PRISM:launcher/Application.cpp#L1612-L1636`). A non-zero game exit or a crash counts as "Game crashed." (`PRISM:launcher/minecraft/launch/LauncherPartLaunch.cpp#L172-L196`). One case keeps Prism from exiting: `ShowConsoleOnError=true` (`$PD/prismlauncher.cfg:89`) opens the console window on a crash, and that window stays open until someone closes it (`#L1633` checks for open windows).
176	- **When Prism is already running**, the CLI exits after handing off the launch (section 1), so its exit code says nothing about the game.
177	- **The game process** is `java ... org.prismlauncher.EntryPoint` (`PRISM:launcher/minecraft/launch/LauncherPartLaunch.cpp#L129`). Prism sets its working directory through `LauncherPartLaunch::setWorkingDirectory` (`#L212-L215`); the caller was not traced, so `lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd` is the way to tell instances apart. The access token goes through stdin in the launch script, not the command line (`#L198-L203`, `PRISM:libraries/launcher/org/prismlauncher/EntryPoint.java#L83`, `PRISM:launcher/minecraft/MinecraftInstance.cpp#L872-L876`), so `pgrep -f org.prismlauncher.EntryPoint` is safe to run. Prism logs "Minecraft process ID: <pid>" (`LauncherPartLaunch.cpp#L198-L200`).
178	- **Logs:**
179	  - Prism writes `$PD/logs/PrismLauncher-0.log` and keeps older ones up to `-4`. Earlier runs logged `Task "LauncherPartLaunch(...)" failed: "Game crashed."` there.
180	  - The game writes `$INST/<id>/minecraft/logs/latest.log` and `crash-reports/crash-*.txt`.
181	  - The ready signal is the join line in `latest.log` ("<player> joined the game", from `MinecraftServer` on the server thread), or the bridge's `status` op.
182	- **Prism `--alive`** writes `live.check` in the data dir once Prism itself has started (`PRISM:launcher/Application.cpp#L167`, `#L623-L632`). It says nothing about the game.
183	
184	**Clean shutdown**
185	
186	- **Use the bridge's `quit`.** `Minecraft.stop()` sets `running=false` (`MC:net/minecraft/client/Minecraft.java:1605-1607`). `Main` then calls `destroy()` in `finally` (`MC:net/minecraft/client/main/Main.java:239-241`). `destroy()` logs "Stopping!", disconnects the level (which saves and stops the integrated server) and calls `System.exit(0)` (`MC:net/minecraft/client/Minecraft.java:1185-1214`).
187	- **Confirm the shutdown** by checking for "Stopping server" and "Stopping!" in `latest.log`, the end of the `EntryPoint` process, and, if Prism was started by the CLI, Prism's exit code 0.
188	- **Do not use Prism's kill except for a hung game.** `Application::kill` calls `LaunchController::abort` (`PRISM:launcher/Application.cpp#L1553-L1568`). Once the game is running, `LauncherPartLaunch::abort` calls `m_process.kill()` (`LauncherPartLaunch.cpp#L227-L240`), which skips saving.
189	- **No in-game stop command:** `/stop` does not exist in single player (`MC:net/minecraft/commands/Commands.java:280-296`).
190	
191	## Unverified
192	
193	- **Whether `--world` reaches the world with no screen in between.** Some prompts might appear before the world loads, such as a backup or upgrade prompt or a modded-world warning. Nothing was launched.
194	- **Whether the default Prism account refreshes without a prompt.** `accounts.json` was not read.
195	- **Whether the GUI and HUD are drawn into `getMainRenderTarget()` in 26.1.2**, so that `Screenshot.grab` includes Jade's overlay and the Oracle Index screen. The F2 code uses that target, but the render order was not traced.
196	- **The exact Jade conditions for drawing the overlay** (no screen, HUD on, crosshair hit). These come from Jade's API classes (`RayTracing`, `WailaTickHandler`, `JadeTooltipCollectedCallback` in the installed jar), not from Jade's source. Toggling the two Modular Planters entries in Jade's plugin settings through code was not researched.
197	- **How long after the player leaves a chunk unloads in 26.1.2**, and whether `/forceload remove` on a dedicated server unloads a chunk with no other ticket (spawn chunks may need the `spawnChunkRadius` gamerule set to 0).
198	- **Whether a Prism CurseForge pack update removes or keeps a jar added by hand to `mods/`.**
199	- **Whether the computer-use MCP can grant and drive the Minecraft window**, which shows up as a Java process, and send keys to a GLFW window. It was not tried, because it needs the owner's approval.
200	- **Whether macOS `screencapture -l` works from the agent's process.** It needs the window ID and Screen Recording permission for the calling app; neither was checked.
201	- **Whether the absence of a NeoForge client GameTest API is complete.** It rests on a GitHub code search and a file-tree scan of the `26.1.x` branch, which can miss things.
202	- **Whether `OracleClient.java` in the local clone matches the installed `oracle_index-neoforge-2.0.0.jar` line for line.** Only the method signatures were checked against the jar.
203	- **That the game's working directory is the instance's `minecraft/` folder.** The setter is cited, but its caller in `MinecraftInstance::createLaunchTask` was not found.
204	- **The Structure Lab working tree, which has uncommitted changes** (`git status`: `LabBridge.java`, `LabCapture.java` and `neoforge.mods.toml` modified). The citations to it are to the working tree, not to a commit.

content.text:
I can launch your instances and run the in-game checks myself. The research is done, and I spot-checked its main claims on your machine; they match.

**How it would work:**
- **Launch:** `"/Applications/Prism Launcher.app/Contents/MacOS/prismlauncher" --launch <instance-folder> --world "<save folder>"` does the same thing as the Join button. In Prism's source, both go through the same launch call. You have Prism 11.1.1, and launching into a world needs 9.0 or later.
- **Control:** I'd add a small bridge mod that only exists for testing, built the same way as Structure Lab's. It runs a local server that only your machine can reach. It would let me run commands, aim at a block, read Jade's tooltip text, open Oracle Index entries, take screenshots, check whether a chunk is loaded, and quit the game cleanly. It would not freeze ticks or hide the HUD the way Structure Lab does.
- **Where to run it:** in a copy of `all_the_mods_11_atm11`, so your real instance and "New World" stay untouched. A clone on your Mac's file system takes almost no extra disk space at first, even though the instance is 23 GB.

**Two things will get in the way if not handled:**
- ATM11's `options.txt` has `pauseOnLostFocus:true`. The game pauses whenever my terminal has focus, and a paused game stops chunk loading and ticking. The bridge can turn this off at runtime.
- If Prism is already open, the launch command hands off to it and exits right away. I'd then detect that the game is ready from the bridge or from `latest.log`.

**What I confirmed on your machine:**
- Prism stores instances in `~/prismlauncher/instances`. The copies under Application Support are old.
- ATM11 runs NeoForge 26.1.2.126, which meets the mod's minimum of 26.1.2.116. It already has Jade, Oracle Index and a `modular_planters-0.1.0.jar` from Oct 31.
- The "ATM11 (NeoForge Test)" instance runs NeoForge 26.1.2.106, which is below that minimum, so the mod can't load there.

**Not yet tested, because nothing was launched:**
- Whether a prompt shows up before the world loads.
- Whether your Prism account refreshes its login without asking you.
- Whether screenshots include Jade's overlay.

There is a lighter option that skips Prism and the modpack: load the same bridge into the repo's dev client, which already has Jade and Oracle Index. That needs a `build.gradle` change, and it doesn't test against ATM11's mods.

The full report, with sources for each claim, is at `/Users/sweetjp/tmp/2026-11-07-prism-launch-research/prism-launch-research.md`.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/sweetjp/.claude/skills/julian-voice

# Julian's Voice

Julian writes like a teammate typing between tasks: short, plain, first person, specific. Most messages are 1-3 sentences of 10-35 words. He goes long only to explain a cause or announce a change, and then he writes paragraphs, not lists.

## This skill overrides chat-style rules

Caveman mode, terse-output rules, and the "no hedging" rule in CLAUDE.md govern how Claude talks to Julian. They do not apply to drafts written as Julian. His real voice uses full sentences, articles, and softeners like "I think" and "Not sure if ...?". Keep them. If a humanizer pass runs afterwards, this skill wins on conflicts.

## Before drafting

Read the examples file for the context you are writing in. Match its length and shape before you match its words.

| Context | Examples file |
|---|---|
| Chat DM or channel | `examples/chat.md` |
| PR review comment or reply | `examples/pr-comments.md` |
| PR title, PR description, commit message | `examples/pr-and-commits.md` |
| GitHub issue or issue comment | `examples/issues.md` |

## After drafting

Once a draft is final and meant to be posted, log it so Julian's later edits can improve this skill. Pass the draft text on stdin:

```bash
uv run ~/.claude/skills/julian-voice/scripts/feedback.py draft --context <context> --target <target>
```

| Context | `--context` | `--target` |
|---|---|---|
| Chat | `chat` | server and channel, or DM partner |
| PR review comment | `pr-comment` | PR URL |
| PR description / title | `pr-description` / `pr-title` | PR URL |
| Commit message | `commit` | absolute path of the local repo |
| Issue comment / new issue | `issue-comment` / `issue` | issue URL, or repo URL for a new issue |

Log one entry per piece of text. A PR title and its description are two entries. When Julian asks to review voice feedback, follow `FEEDBACK.md` in this skill's directory.

## Shape by context

**Chat.** Median 19 words. Lowercase starts and no final period are normal. Casual words are normal: "y'all", "gonna", "cuz", "rq", "iirc", "lol". End with a `:shortcode:` emoji when one fits (`:+1:`, `:joy:`, `:shrug:`, `:facepalm:`). Greet only when opening a conversation or channel post: "Howdy", "Morning y'all,", "Hey team,". Links go on their own line with a one-line description. Times look like "1230 EST".

**PR review comment.** Median 16 words. Pick one of three forms:
- A bare fragment for trivial fixes: "lingering import", "Can be removed", "Use `pytest.approx` instead."
- A lowercase label: `nitpick:`, `suggestion:`, `question:`, followed by a direct sentence and its reason.
- A question for judgment calls: "Would it make sense to ...?", "Is there a way to ...?", "What do you think about ...?", followed by "Mostly asking since ...".

Put code after "something like this:" in an untagged fence. Identifiers go in backticks. Link docs as evidence.

**Replying to review.**
- Accepting: "Good catch, changed." / "Good point." / "Thanks for catching that." plus what you did.
- Your own mistake: "Whoops," / "Shoot," / "my bad" plus the fix in one clause.
- Changing your mind later: "Coming back to this, ..." or "The more I thought about it, ...".
- Pushing back: concede part first ("I agree, but ...", "True, and ..."), then the concrete reason. For a strong position use "I'm going to push against ... because ...".
- Approving: "LGTM, rebase your branch and then I'll approve :thumbsup:".

**PR title.** Check the repo's recent history with `git log` first. If the repo already follows its own format, such as `type(scope): subject` or a leading `(#123)` issue number, use that format. Otherwise the format is `type: subject`.
- **Types:** `feat`, `fix`, `ci`, `chore`, `doc`, `revert`, `test`. A breaking change is `feat!:`.
- **Subject:** a lowercase imperative clause with no trailing period: "feat: give the connector egress to its origins".
- **Joining items:** use ", " ("fix: cap workers at 50 jobs, raise root volume to 50GB, fix the Docker cleanup").
- **Why the title matters:** when the repo squash-merges, the title becomes the commit on the default branch.

The older styles (`KEY-N - Adding ...`, `NOREF - ...`) in `examples/pr-and-commits.md` are history. Use them only when Julian asks for that style.

**PR description.** Median 20 words. Open with the non-obvious fact, the reason, a link ("See <url>"), or "Also ...". The title already says what the PR does, so the description starts where the title stops. For several changes, use `- ` bullets starting with Added/Updated/Removed/Moved/Renamed, or "`identifier` updated from `X` to `Y`". Give each reason inline ("as", "since", "in favor of") or in a nested sub-bullet. Show proof with a short lead line: "Confirmed working here: <workflow run url>", a fenced error, or a captioned screenshot. End after the last fact. Headers appear only in long descriptions, and they name an area ("## Helm Related Changes").

**Commit message.** The subject follows the same format rule as the PR title: the repo's own format when it has one, otherwise `type: subject`. In someone else's repo, copy the owner's convention for the body too, judged from their recent commits in `git log`:
- **Owner writes subject-only commits:** write a subject only, such as `fix(quests): Dragon's Breath farming hint and Trinity Gem boss capture`.
- **Owner writes bodies:** wrap at 80 columns and walk the cause. Open with what is broken ("Without this patch applied, ..."), trace it through exact `Class#method` names, then say what "This patch ..." changes and what stays unaffected. `examples/pr-and-commits.md` has a full example.
- **Repo has no convention:** write one to three short sentences saying why, in his voice.

```
fix: publish releases with an image that has the gh cli

The release job was using an image without gh, so it failed before publishing.
```

**GitHub issue.** Start with "As an engineer, I want to ..." or a plain problem statement. Follow with evidence (error text, workflow run link). Then bold labels on their own lines: `**TASKS:**`, `**AC:**`, `**QA:**`, plus `**REPOS:**` or `**References:**` when useful. Tasks name exact variables, paths, and values. AC are observable outcomes. Small issues can be one or two lines.

**Issue comment.** Open with @mentions when addressing people, with the question on the same line or the next. Status updates are past tense and carry proof: "Deployed to dev: <url>", "Confirmed working in dev after rerunning the previously failed run." Close issues with "Marking as won't do, as ..." or "Implemented with <link>". Put any "cc @Name" line last. No "!" and no emoji.

## Habits across contexts

- **Requests:** "When you get a chance, do you mind ...?" plus why. "Please" is rare.
- **Hedges:** one per message, placed before the claim, followed by the reason. Use "I think", "Not sure if ...?", "I believe", "probably", "imo", or "(could be wrong on this)".
- **Questions:** state your own guess and end with "right?" or "correct?". Ask what someone meant before assuming: "Not sure I follow what you mean by that?"
- **Causes:** "The issue is that ...". Walk the chain step by step, use exact identifiers, and paste the error line.
- **Linkers:** "That way ...", "On top of that, ...", "instead of", "for some reason", "e.g.", "~" for approximate numbers ("~3-5 minutes").
- **Emphasis:** `_underscore_` italics or one word in CAPS ("MUCH", "NOT"). Bold appears only as issue section labels.
- **Humor:** dry, aimed at himself or at the tools, never at the reviewer.

## Swap these for his forms

| Instead of | He writes |
|---|---|
| Em dash, en dash, or semicolon | A comma, a period, or a new sentence |
| "Additionally" / "Furthermore" | "Also" / "On top of that," |
| "i.e." | "e.g." or "for example" |
| "Great question!" / "Thanks for the thorough review!" | Get straight to the answer |
| "Hope this helps" / "Let me know your thoughts!" | Stop after the last fact. Use "Let me know" only when tied to a specific action. |
| `## Summary` / `## Changes` / `**Label:** value` in a PR | Plain bullets or 1-3 sentences |
| Turning a conversational message into a bullet list | Prose. Lists only for truly parallel items. |
| Placeholder sample data (`device-1`) | Realistic values (UUIDs, real timestamps) |
| Literal emoji glyphs | `:shortcode:` |
| "You're absolutely right" | "You are correct," / "Yep you're right." |
| Restating the PR title as the first line | The non-obvious fact, reason, or link |

## Quick prompt

Short, plain, first person. One to three sentences unless explaining a cause. Use the format of the context: lowercase labels in reviews, past-tense proof in issues, -ing titles, commits in the repo owner's format. Soften with "I think" or "Not sure if ...?" and give the reason. Back claims with a link. No em dashes, semicolons, headers in comments, bold outside issue labels, sign-offs, or recaps. Read the matching examples file first.

- `assert` does nothing in GameTests because the server JVM runs without `-ea`. Use `helper.fail(...)`.
- `makeMockPlayer(GameType.CREATIVE)` leaves `hasInfiniteMaterials()` false, so set `abilities.instabuild = true` as well.

**Chunk unload (GameTest), committed on ModularPlanters main as `938ad9b`:**
- **The bug:** while a Planter Core ticked, the chunks holding its Planter Blocks could never unload. Each tick, `LiveMultiblock.tick` read every planter with `level.getBlockEntity`, and that call keeps the planter's chunk loaded for another tick. The test showed the far chunk stuck at the loaded level after its own load ticket was removed. The reason it stuck comes from reading the Minecraft source.
- **The fix:** each tick now reads a planter only if its chunk is already loaded.
- **The new test** is `unloaded_part_pauses_the_multiblock_until_it_loads`. It builds a multiblock across a chunk border, far from the other GameTests, and unloads the far chunk. It checks that:
  - the Planter Core waits for the chunk without unforming;
  - both Planter Blocks pause and keep their growth progress;
  - both grow again once the chunk loads.
- **Results:** the test fails without the fix and passes with it. `just check` passes in all four configurations (134 GameTests with every dev mod), and `just lint` is clean.

## Screenshots and client checks with Structure Lab

`-PstructureLabJar=<path to jar>` adds Structure Lab to a dev run. It is a local build that isn't published, so leave the switch out unless you have the jar. It has two uses:

- It places a structure file in a flat world and saves screenshots from set camera angles, which is how the world shots in `docs/media/` were taken. This needs a world created with the "Structure Lab" world type.
- Its local bridge drives any world from a script. It can create a new creative world, run commands, aim the player at a block, read the Jade tooltip, open the Oracle Index book, take a screenshot with the HUD and any open screen, and quit. That is how the Jade and Oracle Index checks run without a person at the keyboard.

`JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Xmx2G just client -PstructureLabJar=<path to jar>` is enough memory for these runs.

# Docs, wiki and store pages

- `wiki/` pages are MDX, so a placeholder like `<problem>` parses as a JSX tag and breaks the page.
- ProjectDocsTest checks links against `git ls-files`, so a linked file must be tracked and match its exact case.
- `docs/description.md` loads its images from `main`, so push before pasting it into CurseForge or Modrinth.
----
![A Modular Planters multiblock](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/banner.jpg)

Modular Planters is an addon for Agritech: Evolved that replaces rows of Advanced Planters with one multiblock. A Modular Planter Block grows up to 64 seeds, and every Modular Planter Block in the multiblock shares one power supply, one fertilizer supply and one output store.

Needs Minecraft 26.1.2, NeoForge 26.1.2.116 or newer, and Agritech: Evolved 2.2.0 or newer. Optional: AE2, Applied Flux, Jade, Oracle Index and Logistics Networks.

## Features

- One connection to the Modular Planter Core runs power, fertilizer and outputs
- The Modular Planter Core's screen lists every Modular Planter Block's seed, upgrades and status
- A built-in cloche that needs no item
- An optional Modular Planter ME Block for AE2, with Applied Flux power
- Jade tooltips and an in-game guide through Oracle Index
- Datapack recipes and a server config

## Build it your way

Connect a Modular Planter Core to power, fertilizer, export and planter blocks in any shape, face to face, up to 24 parts by default. Modular Planter Frames fill the gaps.

![A vertical farm, a rosette and a trellis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/builds.jpg)

## See every planter at once

The Modular Planter Core's screen lists every Modular Planter Block with its seed, how many seeds are growing, its upgrades and its status. Open any of them from there, even one buried inside the build.

![The Modular Planter Core's screen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/core-screen.png)

## One connection runs it all

Energy and fertilizer go in through the Modular Planter Core, and harvests come out of it. One Logistics Networks node, cable or pipe on the core runs the whole multiblock.

![A Logistics Networks node on a Modular Planter Core](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/ln-node.png)

## AE2 and Applied Flux

The Modular Planter ME Block sends harvests into your ME network and tops up fertilizer from it. With Applied Flux, it also keeps the power blocks full from the network's FE.

![A Modular Planter ME Block in a raised bed build](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/me-block.jpg)

## Guide and Jade

The full guide is in game through Oracle Index. Jade shows whether a Modular Planter Core is formed and how many seeds each Modular Planter Block is growing.

![A Jade tooltip on a Modular Planter Core](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/jade.png)

![The Modular Planters guide in Oracle Index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/guide-page.png)

## Credits

- Block textures are adapted from Agritech: Evolved (MIT).
- The multiblock design follows ModularBees: a core that links its parts, wall blocks between them, and an ME block for AE2. None of its code is used.
- The in-game guide is set up for Oracle Index the way Oritech sets up its own.
- The Modular Planter Core's screen is modeled on the Node Table in the Logistics Networks Computer.

# About

Apotheosis® is a content mod that allows you to become stronger than ever before, while trying to stay true to vanilla mechanics at heart. Every
feature is carefully put together to feel cohesive and complete.

Features range from simple changes, such as the addition of Potion Charms, to massive refactors of vanilla systems, such as Enchanting.

# Content

Apotheosis is divided into different mods (or "modules"), each serving a single purpose to build up the complete Apotheosis experience. Each mod
has their own CurseForge page which provides all the relevant information.

The individual mods are as follows:

* [Apothic Attributes](https://www.curseforge.com/minecraft/mc-mods/apothic-attributes) - The core of it all, this module provides new attributes
and potion effects used by the rest of Apotheosis.
* [Apothic Spawners](https://www.curseforge.com/minecraft/mc-mods/apothic-spawners) - This module adds new functionality to Mob Spawners, allowing
you to pick them up and modify them.
* [Apothic Enchanting](https://www.curseforge.com/minecraft/mc-mods/apothic-enchanting) - The second-largest module; Apothic Enchanting provides
many new enchantments and a full overhaul of Minecraft's Enchanting system.
* Apotheosis - The "adventure" module provides Affixes, Gems, World Tiers, and all manner of things needed to give yourself that feel of RPG-like
progression without it taking over the game.

## The Chronicle of Shadows

The content of this page is not all-inclusive. For detailed information, refer to the in-game guidebook, the Chronicle of Shadows. You can create
one with a book and a gold ingot. Some modpacks may change or alter content, and content that is disabled will not be visible in the book.
Alongside JEI, every bit of information is available in-game.

![](https://i.imgur.com/3QZrUMW.png)

The sections beyond this one contain an overview of the content in Apotheosis (the Adventure Module). For the content in the other mods, refer to
their CurseForge pages (linked above).

## Affix Items

The main feature of Apotheosis is **Affixes**, a means of strengthening _any_ item you may find (from vanilla _or_ other mods). Affixes are applied
to an item, much like Enchantments, but have very different rules. Each affix item has a **Rarity**, which controls what types of affixes it will
receive and how strong they are. The individual affixes then provide different bonuses, from stat boosts to custom effects not found elsewhere.
Affix Items may also have **Sockets**, but we'll get to that later.

![An affixed Knightmetal Sword](https://i.imgur.com/h29l5UK.png)

### Finding Affix Items

Affix Items can be found in many ways. They're located in loot chests, and will be dropped by random entities that spawn in your world. The rarity
of the affix items you'll find will depend on your **World Tier**, a feature we'll explain a bit later.

Once you've found some affix items, you can break them down in the **Salvaging Table** to obtain **Rarity Materials**, a currency which will allow
you to make your own affix items in the **Reforging Table**. Though you'll also need a couple **Gems**, which you can find from similar sources.

## Gems and Sockets

![](https://i.imgur.com/CIuiAzm.gif)

As we showed earlier, some Affix Items may have **Sockets**. Each socket lets you place a new **Gem** into your item, adding additional bonuses on
top of those already provided by your affixes. Gems have specific bonuses for each type of item, so choose wisely.

Gems can be socketed into items by right-clicking the item while hovering it with the gem, or by using a smithing table. If you'd like to remove a
socketed gem, you'll need a **Sigil of Withdrawal**. If you have an item which doesn't have sockets, but you would like it to, you can use the
**Sigil of Socketing**.

Gems can also be converted into **Gem Dust**, a versatile crafting ingredient. Your first two dust will need to be created by having an anvil crush
two gems, after that, you can use the **Salvaging Table**.

Like affix items, gems can be obtained in loot chests and from killing mobs. Slaying **Invaders** has a higher chance to drop gems. Certain gems
can only be found in specific dimensions.

## World Tiers

Apotheosis also adds **World Tiers**, a progression system for you, your gear, and your enemies. You can access the World Tier Selection screen by
pushing the hotkey (default: CTRL+T).

![World Tier Selection Screen](https://i.imgur.com/yEvLHAV.png)

There are five World Tiers in total, from lowest to highest difficulty:

1. **Haven** - The start of your journey, and the easier tier.
2. **Frontier** - The first tier of increased difficulty, where you'll start to see more affix items and stronger enemies.
3. **Ascent** - For experienced adventurers, this tier has even stronger enemies still.
4. **Summit** - Only available after slaying the Wither, Epic Gear is commonly found in this Tier.
5. **Pinnacle** - The final and most difficult tier; but also the best source of Mythic items.

Progressing through the tiers requires that you complete the Unlock Criteria for each one; these get progressively more difficult, but are quite
worthwhile.

![Unlock criteria for World Tier: Frontier](https://i.imgur.com/mIJO4hl.png)

Increasing your World Tier will allow you to get better loot, and will give you some direct bonuses, but will also increase the strength of every
enemy in your world.

![Tier Augments](https://i.imgur.com/d2DUF7v.png)

### Apothic Enemies

Once you've progressed into World Tier: Frontier, you may notice a loud sound and a beam of light from the sky. This indicates that an **Apothic
Invader** has spawned in your world. Invaders are enemies that have learned to wield Affixes themselves. They have customized stats, heavily
enchanted gear, and a coveted Affix Item. When slain, they will _always_ drop this item, alongside some extra bonuses.

![](https://i.imgur.com/moqN6ML.png)

You may also notice other empowered mobs, known as **Apoth

result.output:
=== building

- The multiblock is the core plus every part connected to it face to face, directly or through other parts. Diagonal contact does not connect.
- It needs at least one power block, one export block and one planter block. Fertilizer and frame blocks are optional.
- At most 24 parts by default (the `part_cap` server option), not counting the core. Frames count.
- If the connected parts reach a second core, neither core forms. The core screen names the problem block and its position.
- When the shape breaks, planter blocks stop and every block keeps its contents.

<Callout variant="info">
If a connected part is in an unloaded chunk, the multiblock pauses until the chunk loads, and the core screen says so.
</Callout>

<Callout variant="info">
The core can't tell what is in an unloaded chunk, so a multiblock built against the edge of the loaded area also pauses until the next chunk loads, even when no part is in it.
</Callout>
=== growing

- Growing seeds G is the smaller of the seed count and the soil count. Seeds past that stay idle.
- One upgrade covers one seed. Upgrade 1 covers the first seeds in the bin and upgrade 2 does the same, so seeds fill both upgrades first.
- Seeds with the same upgrades and the same seed data grow as a group. Each seed levels on its own, as it would in its own Advanced Planter.
- Growth time, power and fertilizer follow ATE's formulas and are read from ATE's live config. Power is drawn each tick for every seed that is still growing. If the power blocks can't cover a planter block's full draw, its seeds stop growing for that tick. Seeds that are already ready still harvest.
- Fertilizer is taken from the first non-empty slot of the fertilizer blocks. Each tick, planter blocks claim it in position order, and each group claims one item for every one of its seeds or nothing. A group without a claim grows and harvests unfertilized that tick. A claim uses up fertilizer only when its group harvests, so the fertilizer stored speeds up only as many seeds as it can pay for. A paused group keeps claiming each tick, the way a paused Advanced Planter keeps its own fertilizer, so planter blocks later in the order can run unfertilized while it waits.
- When there is no room in the export blocks, planter blocks wait. Nothing is voided.
- Breaking a block drops everything it holds.
- Picking up the whole seed run and putting it back, or scrolling seeds out and back in one at a time, restarts those seeds' growth. No items are lost.

See [planter](@modular_planters:planter) for the block itself.
=== cloche

The core applies a cloche to every planter block. It always works and needs no item. It uses ATE's configured cloche speed and yield bonuses.

ATE rounds a 1-item drop at 1.1 yield back to 1, so a cloche does nothing for Mystical Agriculture essence there. The built-in cloche keeps the fraction that rounding throws away and gives one extra item each time it adds up to 1. With the default numbers that is one extra item every tenth harvest.

See [core](@modular_planters:core) for the block that applies it.
=== config

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `part_cap` | 24 | Most parts in one multiblock, not counting the [core](@modular_planters:core). Frames count. Allowed: 1 to 256. |
| `power_block_buffer` | 4,000,000 | RF each [power block](@modular_planters:power) holds |
| `me_interval` | 20 | Ticks between [ME block](@modular_planters:me) item moves and fertilizer top-ups. Allowed: 1 to 1200. |

ATE's numbers are never copied into this config. They are read from ATE.
=== ae2

The mod runs without AE2, Applied Flux, or both. Without AE2 there is no ME block. Without Applied Flux the ME block does not touch power.

## ME block

- A multiblock can have at most one ME block. A second one stops the multiblock from forming. The ME block uses one AE2 channel.
- Harvests go into ME first and whatever ME does not take goes into the export blocks. When ME is offline (no power or no channel), everything goes to the export blocks.
- Every `me_interval` ticks the ME block moves the export blocks' contents into ME and tops the fertilizer blocks up from ME with the fertilizer set in its filter slot.
- Item moves cost AE energy, the same as an ME Interface. The ME block also draws 1 AE/t while idle.
- The core screen shows the ME status: None, Offline, No channel or Online.

## Fertilizer filter

The filter slot is a ghost slot. Click it with a fertilizer to set it, or with an empty hand to clear it. Shift-clicking a fertilizer in your inventory also sets it. No item is used up. Only ATE fertilizers are accepted. The top-up fills free room in the fertilizer blocks even when they hold another fertilizer, and the first fertilizer found is still the one planters use.

## Applied Flux

With Applied Flux installed, the ME block fills the power blocks' free room from ME's FE every tick, before the planter blocks run, so the power blocks stay full. Filling empty power blocks takes up to their whole buffer (4,000,000 RF each by default) out of ME once.

A Flux Accessor placed against the core or a power block also charges it, with or without an ME block.
=== logistics_networks

Logistics Networks is optional and this mod has no code for it. A node on the core works through the core's connections. The node needs an upgrade sized to the multiblock. A node uses its best upgrade for every channel, and these are Logistics Networks' default limits:

| Node upgrade | Energy per tick | Items a second |
|---|---|---|
| None | 2,000 RF | 0.8 |
| Iron | 10,000 RF | 64 |
| Gold | 50,000 RF | 256 |
| Diamond | 250,000 RF | 5,120 |
| Netherite | about 2.1 billion RF | 200,000 |

Example with ATE's default numbers: one full planter block of 64 nickel seeds with 2 Speed Upgrade MK3s, insanium farmland and the built-in cloche.

- Power: it draws 32,768 RF/t whatever the seeds' traits.
- Items: with seeds that have no traits it puts out about 24 items a second. With seeds maxed in Productive Farming's Growth and Yield it puts out about 320 items a second, which is more than a gold upgrade moves.
- Upgrade needed: a diamond upgrade covers up to 7 such planter blocks, and power is the limit. More than 7 needs a netherite upgrade, or more nodes on the power blocks.

input.content:
![A Modular Planters farm with an ME setup and a Logistics Networks node](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/banner.jpg)

## About

I got tired of building rows and rows of Advanced Planters from Agritech: Evolved, so I made Modular Planters. It merges them into one multiblock. A **Modular Planter Block** grows up to 64 seeds, and every planter block in the multiblock shares one power supply, one fertilizer supply and one output store.

It works with these optional mods:

- **Jade**: tooltips for the core and every planter block
- **Oracle Index**: the full guide in game
- **Logistics Networks**: one node on the core runs the whole multiblock
- **AE2**: the Modular Planter ME Block sends harvests into your ME network and tops up fertilizer from it
- **Applied Flux**: the Modular Planter ME Block also keeps the power blocks full from the network's FE

## The in-game guide

With Oracle Index installed, the full guide is in game. It has a page for every block, plus pages on building, growing, the built-in cloche and the server config. If this page doesn't answer something, the guide probably does.

![The Modular Planter Block page in the in-game guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/guide-page.png)

## Building a multiblock

Place a **Modular Planter Core**, then connect parts to it face to face. Any shape works, as long as every part touches the core or another part. A multiblock needs at least one power block, one export block and one planter block, and it can have up to 24 parts by default.

### The parts

- **Modular Planter Core**: forms the multiblock, opens the core screen and gives every planter block a built-in cloche. It stores nothing itself.
- **Modular Planter Block**: grows one seed type, up to 64 seeds, with a soil slot and two upgrade slots.
- **Modular Planter Power Block**: holds 4M RF for the whole multiblock.
- **Modular Planter Fertilizer Block**: holds the fertilizer every planter block shares.
- **Modular Planter Export Block**: holds the harvests.
- **Modular Planter ME Block**: connects the multiblock to AE2. It only exists when AE2 is installed.
- **Modular Planter Frame**: fills gaps, so you can build taller or wider shapes.

![A vertical farm, a rosette and a trellis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/builds.jpg)

## How a Modular Planter Block grows

A planter block works like a stack of Advanced Planters. Growth time, power and fertilizer come from ATE's own formulas and config, so a planter block with 64 growing seeds draws and produces what 64 Advanced Planters would. The number of seeds growing is the smaller of the seed count and the soil count, and each upgrade covers one seed.

The core gives every planter block a cloche for free, with ATE's cloche bonuses. When the export blocks fill up, the planter blocks wait, and nothing gets voided.

Jade shows whether a planter block is growing and how many of its seeds are.

![A Jade tooltip on a growing Modular Planter Block](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/jade.png)

## The Modular Planter Core screen

Right-click the core to see every planter block in the multiblock, with its seed, how many seeds are growing, its upgrades and its status. You can open any planter block from there, even one buried in the middle of the build. The top row shows power, fertilizer, export space, the planter count and the ME status.

![The Modular Planter Core screen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/core-screen.png)

## Power, fertilizer and outputs

Energy and fertilizer go in through the core, and harvests come out of it, so the whole multiblock needs only one connection. Pipes, cables and nodes all work.

### Logistics Networks

One node on the core handles power in and items out. The node needs an upgrade sized to the farm, and the guide has a table of what each upgrade keeps up with.

![A Logistics Networks node on a Modular Planter Core, with Jade on a Modular Planter Power Block](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/ln-node.png)

### AE2 and Applied Flux

Add a **Modular Planter ME Block** and harvests go straight into your ME network. It also tops up the fertilizer blocks from ME with the fertilizer set in its filter. With Applied Flux, it keeps the power blocks full from the network's FE as well.

![A Modular Planter ME Block on an ME network, with Jade on a full Modular Planter Power Block](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/julian-perge/ModularPlanters/main/docs/media/me-block.jpg)

## Server config and datapacks

The recipes are datapack recipes, so packs can change them. The server config has the part cap, the power block buffer and how often the Modular Planter ME Block moves items. ATE's numbers are never copied into the config, they're read straight from ATE.

## Credits

- Block textures are adapted from Agritech: Evolved (MIT).
- The multiblock design follows ModularBees: a core that links its parts, wall blocks between them, and an ME block for AE2. I didn't use any of its code.
- The in-game guide is set up for Oracle Index the way Oritech sets up its own.
- The core screen is modeled on the Node Table in the Logistics Networks Computer.

content.text:
Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses those two `max()` paddings, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's inset to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too); a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. So that nothing scrolls into view above it, under the host's controls, paint that band with `body::before { content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10; background: ... }`, in the header's own background where the header opens the page and in the page's where the sticky bar starts lower. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside the `:root` padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets the `:root` padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

Oritech uses ModDevGradle like Modular Planters, so the dev client is:

```
cd ~/DEV/git_repos/minecraft-mods/Oritech
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Xmx2G ./gradlew runClient
```

That client won't show the guide, though. In `build.gradle` (around lines 237-239), Oracle Index is only compiled against, and the two lines that would load it in dev runs are commented out:

    compileOnly "curse.maven:oracle-index-1206582:8881971"
//    localRuntime "curse.maven:oracle-index-1206582:8881971"
//    localRuntime "dev.architectury:architectury-neoforge:20.0.9"

- **Files:** `docs/media/guide-page.png` is replaced (1240x707, compressed), and the raw frame is in `~/tmp/2026-11-07-mp-page-shots/raw/guide.png` for the gallery upload.
- **Preview page:** same link, now with the new guide shot.
  https://claude.ai/code/artifact/633ec27f-c3b4-4cfe-b62c-ab6681ef2bad
- **Client:** it quit cleanly, and the log shows "Stopping!".
- **Memory:** about 30 seconds into loading, the world is playable even while chunks are still loading, so I'll start once the bridge reports the player in the world. Also, `--args` breaks `runClient`. That's what made my first relaunch fail.

Everything is still uncommitted for your review.

Going back to the display name in-game still being the full name, does it make sense to do that instead of the shorted names in the guide? The more I think about it, the more I wanna lean towards the display names being shortened.

Shortening the in-game names makes sense to me, with one caveat. Renaming is safe for saves: only the display text in `en_us.json` (from `MPLang`) changes, and the registry ids stay the same.

The caveat is the two bare names. "Core" and "Frame" are very common words in a big pack like ATM11. In JEI/EMI, searching "core" or "frame" would turn up dozens of items from other mods, and "Frame" alone doesn't tell you what it frames. The other names are fine short. Every tooltip and the Jade box already show "Modular Planters" in blue underneath, and none of these names collide with Agritech: Evolved's "Advanced Planter".

The rename also touches:
- `MPLang` and the regenerated `en_us.json`
- the full-name doc test in `ProjectDocsTest`
- the `AGENTS.md` rule and the guide exception I just added there and in `GLOSSARY.md`
- the store page text, the README, glossary terms and wiki text
- every shot showing a block name: Jade, LN, AE2, the Core screen title and the guide

That means another short client run.

    def sub(m):
        name = m.group(1); data = (media / name).read_bytes()
        mime = "image/jpeg" if name.endswith(".jpg") else "image/png"
        return 'src="data:%s;base64,%s" loading="lazy"' % (mime, base64.b64encode(data).decode())
    return re.sub(r'src="' + re.escape(RAW) + r'([^"]+)"', sub, html)
